title: DACA Renewal Delays Leave Thousands of Immigrants Unable to Work
excerpt: Processing times have surged from 15 days to over four months, stripping work permits from recipients who filed on time and prompting lawsuits against USCIS.
body:
• Median DACA renewal processing times climbed from roughly 15 days in fiscal year 2025 to 122 days by late April 2026, with many cases exceeding five months.
  • Because DACA offers no automatic work-permit extension, recipients who filed on time are losing jobs in healthcare, education and other critical sectors while waiting for approvals.
  • Legal aid groups have sued the Trump administration in federal court seeking data on renewal backlogs and processing hold policies.
  • Utah Sen. John Curtis introduced a bipartisan bill to let states sponsor their own worker visas, calling current labor shortages unsustainable.

Hundreds of thousands of immigrants shielded from deportation under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program are confronting an escalating crisis: processing delays so severe that even those who renewed on time are losing their legal right to work in the United States.

The median wait time for DACA renewals rose from about 15 days in fiscal year 2025 to roughly 70 days by February 2026, according to USCIS data reported by CNN. By late April, the median had climbed to 122 days. Immigration attorneys say most of their clients are now waiting more than four months, with some cases stretching past five months.

A System That Punishes Compliance

Unlike many other immigration benefits, DACA does not provide an automatic extension of work authorization while a renewal is pending. USCIS recommends filing between 150 and 120 days before expiration, but at current processing speeds, even applicants who file at the earliest recommended date risk a gap in their status.

https://x.com/PNS_News/status/2084799099950285147

"This is a dramatic increase in people dealing with incredibly long, and disruptive delays… we are seeing somewhere between a 400% and 1000% increase in processing times."

— Todd Schulte, President, FWD.us

When a work permit lapses, the cascade is swift. Employers face legal liability under federal regulations if they do not re-verify authorization, and many choose termination. In states like Illinois, a lost Employment Authorization Document also triggers a downgrade to a temporary visitor driver's license — a category that federal law allows ICE to query.

Real-World Toll on Workers and Employers

CNN reported the case of a 26-year-old medical school graduate, identified by the pseudonym Marco, who filed for renewal in December 2025 and was still waiting months later. Without an approved renewal, he could not begin his residency in anesthesiology — a delay threatening more than $100,000 in student loan payments.

Maria Fuentes, a 36-year-old registered nurse in Kentucky, lost nearly two months of wages — approximately $9,000 — while her work permit sat in the backlog. Her employer, TJ Samson Community Hospital, wrote to USCIS that the hospital relied on her "full-time availability to maintain safe staffing levels," but held her position until her renewal came through. Other employers have been less patient: a postpartum nurse in Houston, an IT healthcare manager in the Bay Area and a retail manager of seven years all told CNN they were terminated.

More than 90 percent of DACA recipients over 25 are employed. They earn roughly $27.9 billion a year and pay more than $4 billion in state, local and federal taxes, according to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy and the Center for American Progress. The Coalition for the American Dream estimates that 37,000 healthcare workers alone could be lost if the work-permit crisis deepens, eliminating up to $32 billion in projected lifetime earnings.

Enhanced Vetting and Travel-Ban Holds

USCIS has attributed the slowdown to "strengthened screening and vetting" measures. On April 28, the agency announced an enhanced process requiring re-submission of fingerprint-based background checks through an expanded FBI system, temporarily pausing immigration decisions, according to an internal memo viewed by CNN.

Compounding the delays, presidential proclamations issued in June and December 2025 placed processing holds on benefit applications from nationals of 39 countries. An estimated 3,000 to 4,000 DACA recipients are subject to these country-of-origin holds, and the freeze does not pause the clock on expiring work permits.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act has also raised DACA filing fees to $555 for online applications, while eliminating fee waivers that lower-income recipients previously relied on.

Legal Challenges and Legislative Moves

In late June, two legal aid organizations filed suit in the Northern District of California demanding data on renewal timelines and the rationale for processing holds, according to NBC News and EdSource. The groups had submitted information requests in May asking why applicants from October and November 2025 were still waiting. They sued after USCIS missed a June deadline to respond.

"For the years that DACA has been in place, renewals have been fairly reliable. But now, for so many months, we're seeing these delays cause people to fall out of status — that means that folks are losing their jobs."

— Hillary Li, Attorney, Justice Action Center

Meanwhile, Utah Sen. John Curtis introduced a bipartisan bill on August 3 alongside Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly that would allow states to run their own worker visa programs, capped at 5,000 visas per state per fiscal year with additional slots from a 245,000-visa national pool. The bill includes a pathway to legal residency for undocumented immigrants who have been in the country since December 2016, provided they pass background checks and pay a $1,000 penalty.

What's Next

The DACA program itself remains legally fragile. A Fifth Circuit ruling in January 2025 found portions of the Biden-era DACA rule unlawful, and further court action from the Southern District of Texas could restrict operations further. Roughly 506,000 individuals hold DACA status nationwide, according to the Migration Policy Institute.

For now, immigration attorneys recommend filing renewals as early as possible — ideally 150 days before expiration — and consulting legal counsel about contingency planning. But as processing times continue to climb and courts weigh the program's future, the gap between policy and protection keeps widening.
nri_angle: Indian DACA recipients and H-1B workers in states like Utah face compounding uncertainty as both temporary protection programs and the broader legal immigration system slow under enhanced vetting.
